section.heading: 7. Additional Topics in Integration
Introduction
section.paragraph: Besides the basic rules of integration developed in Chapter 6, there are more sophisticated techniques for finding the antiderivatives of functions. We begin this chapter by looking at the method of integration by parts. We then look at a technique of integration that involves using tables of integrals. We also look at numerical methods of integration, which enable us to obtain approximations to definite integrals, especially those whose exact value cannot be found. Numerical integration methods are especially useful when the integrand is known only at discrete points. We also learn how to evaluate integrals in which the intervals of integration are unbounded. Such integrals, called improper integrals, play an important role in the study of probability. Finally, we see how the definite integral can be used to help us find the volume of a solid of revolution.

section.heading: 7.1. Integration by Parts
The Method of Integration by Parts
section.paragraph: Integration by parts is another technique of integration that, like the method of substitution discussed in Chapter 6, is based on a corresponding rule of differentiation. In this case, the rule of differentiation is the Product Rule, which asserts that if $$f$$ and $$g$$ are differentiable functions, then
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack {f{(x)}g(x)} \right\rbrack = f(x)g^{\prime}(x) + g(x)f^{\prime}(x)$$
If we integrate both sides of Equation (1) with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain

$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\int{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}f(x)g(x)dx}} & = & {{\int{f(x)g^{\prime}(x)dx}} + {\int{g(x)f^{\prime}(x)dx}}} \\ {f(x)g(x)} & = & {{\int{f(x)g^{\prime}(x)dx}} + {\int{g(x)f^{\prime}(x)dx}}} \end{array}$$
This last equation, which may be written in the form
$${\int{f(x)}}g^{\prime}(x)dx = {f(x)}g(x) - {\int{g(x)}}f^{\prime}(x)dx$$

is called the formula for integration by parts. This formula is useful because it enables us to express one indefinite integral in terms of another, which may be easier to evaluate. Formula (2) may be simplified by letting
$$\begin{array}{rcllrcl} u & = & {f(x)} & & \mathit{dv} & = & {g^{\prime}(x)dx} \\ \mathit{du} & = & {f^{\prime}(x)dx} & & v & = & {g(x)} \end{array}$$
giving the following version of the formula for integration by parts.

section.heading: 7.2. Integration Using Tables of Integrals
A Table of Integrals
section.paragraph: We have studied several techniques for finding an antiderivative of a function. However, useful as they are, these techniques are not always applicable. There are numerous other methods for finding an antiderivative of a function. Extensive lists of integration formulas have been compiled based on these methods.

Other situations also arise in which an integrable function has an antiderivative that cannot be found in terms of elementary functions (functions that can be expressed as a finite combination of algebraic, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions). Examples of such functions are

Riemann sums provide us with a good approximation of a definite integral, provided that the number of subintervals in the partitions is large enough. But there are better techniques and formulas, called quadrature formulas, that give a more efficient way of computing approximate values of definite integrals. In this section, we look at two rather simple but effective ways of approximating definite integrals.
section.heading: The Trapezoidal Rule
section.paragraph: We assume that $$f(x) \geq 0$$ on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ to simplify the derivation of the Trapezoidal Rule, but the result is valid without this restriction. We begin by subdividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$\Delta x$$ , by means of the $$\left( {n + 1} \right)$$ points $$x_{0} = a,x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ , where $$n$$ is a positive integer (Figure 3).

section.paragraph: Then the length of each subinterval is given by
$$\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$$
Furthermore, as we saw earlier, we may view the definite integral

as the area of the region $$R$$ under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ . This area is given by the sum of the areas of the $$n$$ nonoverlapping subregions $$R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}$$ , where $$R_{1}$$ represents the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = x_{0}$$ to $$x = x_{1}$$ , and so on.

The basis for the Trapezoidal Rule lies in the approximation of each region, $$R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{n}$$ by a suitable trapezoid. This often leads to a much better approximation than one obtained by means of rectangles (a Riemann sum).

Let’s consider the subregion $$R_{1}$$ , shown magnified for the sake of clarity in Figure 4. Observe that the area of the region $$R_{1}$$ may be approximated by the trapezoid of width $$\Delta x$$ whose parallel sides are of lengths $$f\left( x_{0} \right)$$ and $$f\left( x_{1} \right)$$ . The area of the trapezoid is given by
$${\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{0} \right) + f\left( x_{1} \right)}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x} {{Average of the lengths of the parallel sides} \times {width}}$$

section.paragraph: Similarly, the area of the region $$R_{2}$$ may be approximated by the trapezoid of width $$\Delta x$$ and sides of lengths $$f\left( x_{1} \right)$$ and $$f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ . The area of the trapezoid is given by
$$\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right)}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x$$
Continuing, we see that the area of the last ( $$n$$ th) approximating trapezoid is given by
$$\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x$$
Then the area of the region $$R$$ is approximated by the sum of the areas of the $$n$$ trapezoids—that is,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left\lbrack \frac{f{(x_{0})} + f{(x_{1})}}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x + \left\lbrack \frac{f{(x_{1})} + f{(x_{2})}}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x + \ldots + \left\lbrack \frac{f{(x_{n - 1})} + f{(x_{n})}}{2} \right\rbrack \Delta x} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{2}\left\lbrack {f{(x_{0})} + f{(x_{1})} + f{(x_{1})} + f{(x_{2})} + \ldots + f{(x_{n - 1})} + f{(x_{n})}} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{2}\left\lbrack {f{(x_{0})} + 2f{(x_{1})} + 2f{(x_{2})} + \ldots + 2f{(x_{n - 1})} + f{(x_{n})}} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$
Since the area of the region $$R$$ is given by the value of the definite integral we wished to approximate, we are led to the following approximation formula, which is called the Trapezoidal Rule.

section.heading: Simpson’s Rule
section.paragraph: Before stating Simpson’s Rule, let’s review the two rules we have used in approximating a definite integral. Let $$f$$ be a continuous, nonnegative function defined on the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Suppose the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is partitioned by means of the $$n + 1$$ equally spaced points $$x_{0} = a,x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ where $$n$$ is a positive integer, so that the length of each subinterval is $$\Delta x = {\left( {b - a} \right) \slash n}$$ (Figure 5).

The region below the curve is segmented by the perpendiculars dropped from the path of the curve to the tick marks x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3, x_n minus 1, and x_n each in the x axis. The region between the tick marks a = x_0 and x_1 is labeled R_1, x_1 and x_2 is labeled R_2, x_2 and x_3 labeled is R_3, x_n minus 1 and x_n = b is labeled R_n.

section.paragraph: Let’s concentrate on the portion of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ defined on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ . When we use a Riemann sum to approximate the definite integral, we are in effect approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ by the constant function $$y = f\left( p_{1} \right)$$ , where $$p_{1}$$ is chosen to be a point in $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ ; and we are approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by the constant function $$y = f\left( p_{2} \right)$$ , where $$p_{2}$$ lies in $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ . Using a Riemann sum, we see that the area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ between $$x = x_{0}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ is approximated by the area of the region under the approximating “step” function (Figure 6a).

section.paragraph: When we use the Trapezoidal Rule, we are in effect approximating the function $$f(x)$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ by a linear function through the two points $$\left( {x_{0},f\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by a linear function through the two points $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x_{2},f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right)$$ . Thus, the Trapezoidal Rule simply approximates the actual area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = x_{0}$$ to $$x = x_{2}$$ by the area of the region under the approximating polygonal curve (Figure 6b).

A natural extension of the preceding idea is to approximate portions of the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ by means of portions of the graphs of second-degree polynomials (parts of parabolas). It can be shown that given any three noncollinear points, there is a unique parabola that passes through the given points. Choose the points $$\left( {x_{0},f\left( x_{0} \right)} \right)$$ , $$\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {x_{2},f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right)$$ corresponding to the first three points of the partition. Then we can approximate the function $$f(x)$$ on $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ by means of a quadratic function whose graph contains these three points (Figure 7).

section.paragraph: Although we will not do so here, it can be shown that the area of the region under the parabola between $$x = x_{0}$$ and $$x = x_{2}$$ is given by
$$\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right\rbrack$$

Repeating this argument on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{2},x_{4}} \right\rbrack$$ , we see that the area of the region under the curve between $$x = x_{2}$$ and $$x = x_{4}$$ is approximated by the area of the region under the parabola between $$x_{2}$$ and $$x_{4}$$ —that is, by
$$\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + f\left( x_{4} \right)} \right\rbrack$$

Proceeding, we conclude that if $$n$$ is even (Why?), then the area of the region under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ may be approximated by the sum of the areas of the regions under the $$n \slash 2$$ approximating parabolas—that is,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right)} \right\rbrack + \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + f\left( x_{4} \right)} \right\rbrack + \cdots + \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{n - 2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + f\left( x_{4} \right) + \cdots + f\left( x_{n - 2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + 2f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + 2f\left( x_{4} \right) + \cdots + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$
The preceding is the derivation of the approximation formula known as Simpson’s Rule.

list.item: The integration by parts formula is obtained by reversing the Product Rule. The formula for integration by parts is $$\int{udv =}$$ $$uv - {\int{vdu}}$$ . To find $$I = {\int{x\ln{({x^{2} + 1})}dx}}$$ using the table of integrals, we need to first use the substitution rule with $$u =$$ $$x^{2} + 1$$ , so that $$du =$$ $$2xdx$$ to transform $$I$$ into the integral $$I = \frac{1}{2}{\int{u\ln udu}}$$ . We then choose Formula $$(27)$$ to evaluate this integral.

The Trapezoidal Rule states that $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx \approx}$$ $$\frac{\Delta x}{2}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 2f\left( x_{1} \right) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + 2f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)} \right\rbrack$$ where $$\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$$ . The error $$E_{n}$$ in approximating $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}$$ by the Trapezoidal Rule satisfies $$\left| E_{n} \right| \leq$$ $$\frac{M\left( {b - a} \right)^{3}}{12n^{2}}$$ .

Simpson’s Rule states that $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx \approx}$$ $${\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{0} \right) + 4f\left( x_{1} \right) + 2f\left( x_{2} \right) + 4f\left( x_{3} \right) + 2f\left( x_{4} \right)} \right.}{+ \cdot \cdot \cdot + 4f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) + f\left( x_{n} \right)}\rbrack$$ where $$\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}$$ and $$n$$ is even. The error $$E_{n}$$ in approximating $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}$$ by Simpson’s Rule satisfies $$\left| E_{n} \right| \leq$$ $$\frac{M\left( {b - a} \right)^{5}}{180n^{4}}$$ .
